report:
Your “no” is not supported: for osteoporosis, denosumab (Prolia) **does reduce vertebral-fracture risk while treatment is maintained**. The pivotal FREEDOM randomized placebo-controlled trial in 7,868 postmenopausal women found denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months cut new radiographic vertebral fractures from **7.2% with placebo to 2.3%**—about a **68% relative reduction** (RR ~0.32), with hip and nonvertebral fractures also reduced. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19671655/

The absolute benefit was ~4.9 percentage points over 3 years (roughly one vertebral fracture prevented per ~20 treated women), larger in higher-risk patients. Longer-term extension data to 10 years show persistently low fracture incidence and continued BMD gains, but lack a placebo control, so they support durability rather than prove long-term superiority. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/

Key caveat: benefit depends on continuity. After stopping denosumab, bone turnover rebounds and **multiple vertebral fractures have been reported**; labels advise evaluating benefit/risk and transitioning to another antiresorptive if discontinuing. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/125320s186lbl.pdf

Bottom line: evidence says **yes**, with an important “don’t stop abruptly” caveat.
